questions.q: As defined in the lesson, what is bias in an AI system's output?
options: Outputs that systematically favor or disfavor a group, independent of what the model is actually meant to measure
Any output a user personally disagrees with
A model that runs slower than expected
A model that only works for one programming language
questions.explain: The lesson defines bias as systematic favoring or disfavoring of a group, not simple disagreement or performance issues.

questions.q: According to the lesson, how can an AI system create privacy risk without a traditional data breach?
options: The model itself can memorize and reproduce pieces of training data, or combine outputs in a way that re-identifies someone
Privacy risk only ever happens through a stolen laptop
AI systems are incapable of handling personal data in any form
Privacy risk requires a government investigation to exist at all
questions.explain: The lesson explains that memorization and re-identification through outputs mean the model itself can become the exposure.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of a security risk specific to AI systems, per the lesson?
options: Data poisoning that corrupts a model during training
A power outage affecting the office building
An employee forgetting their email password
A printer running out of toner
questions.explain: Data poisoning, along with adversarial inputs and prompt injection, is one of the AI-specific security risks the lesson names.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say hallucination is particularly dangerous?
options: The output is confident and fluent, giving no signal to the reader that it should be double-checked
Hallucinated output is always written in all capital letters
It only occurs in traditional, rule-based software
It can only happen once per day per system
questions.explain: The lesson emphasizes that the confident tone of hallucinated output is what makes it dangerous — it looks just as trustworthy as a correct answer.

questions.q: What does the lesson say about the relationship between the four risk categories?
options: They aren't independent — for example, a biased training set can also create a privacy problem
They are entirely unrelated and never interact
Only one of the four can occur in a single system at a time
They apply only to generative AI, never to other kinds of models
questions.explain: The lesson notes the four categories can overlap and compound, such as biased data also raising privacy concerns.
